comparisons.peer_topic: Noninterest expense increase drivers and prior year comparisons
comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses and investments in people, operations, and technology, partially offset by higher FDIC expense in 2023 (including a $2.1 billion special assessment) and lower expenses from a liquidating business activity.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America disclose that FDIC special assessment fees were a significant, non-recurring driver of operating expense volatility in the 2023-2024 period, though with opposite trends in expense recognition. Goldman Sachs recognized an incremental $71 million in 2024 but benefited from the absence of the large 2023 $529 million fee, contributing to a net decrease in operating expenses. Conversely, Bank of America reported a year-over-year increase in noninterest expense in 2024, but explicitly noted that this increase was partially offset by the absence of the large $2.1 billion FDIC expense accrual from 2023, meaning the comparison of normalized expenses would likely show a decrease similar to GS, despite the headline increase. Additionally, both firms cite higher compensation and revenue-related expenses as offsetting drivers against these regulatory fee benefits.

sentences.text: Operating expenses, compared with 2023, reflected decreases driven by significantly lower expenses, including impairments ($1.46 billion recognized in 2023), related to commercial real estate in CIEs (largely in depreciation and amortization) and other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including the write-down of identifiable intangible assets related to GreenSky of $506 million and an impairment of goodwill related to Consumer platforms of $504 million (both in depreciation and amortization), and the FDIC special assessment fee of $529 million (in other expenses).

An incremental expense for the FDIC special assessment fee of $71 million was recognized in 2024, as the FDIC notified banks subject to the special assessment fee of the updated estimated cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund resulting from the closures in 2023 of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.
Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023.

The increase was primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses as well as investments in people, operations and technology, partially offset by higher Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) expense in 2023, including $2.1 billion for the estimated special assessment amount arising from the closure of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, and lower expenses related to a liquidating business activity.

comparisons.peer_summary: Citigroup's operating expenses decreased 4% to $54.0 billion in 2024, with a 2% decrease to $53.8 billion excluding FDIC special assessments. The decline was driven by organizational simplification savings, reduced restructuring charges, and repositioning costs, partially offset by higher volume-related expenses and costs associated with a July 2024 Civil Money Penalty Consent Order.
comparisons.comparison: Citigroup and Goldman Sachs both highlight the dramatic year-over-year decrease in FDIC special assessment charges as a key factor in their 2024 operating expense profiles. Goldman Sachs recognized a small incremental $71 million in 2024 compared to $529 million in 2023, while Citigroup recognized $203 million in 2024 compared to approximately $1.7 billion in 2023. Both firms use this variance to explain parts of their total operating expense movements, alongside other items. Goldman Sachs focuses on impairments and goodwill write-downs as the primary drivers of its decrease, whereas Citigroup emphasizes organizational simplification savings and reduced restructuring charges, but both explicitly exclude or detail the FDIC assessment impacts to provide context on underlying expense trends.

An incremental expense for the FDIC special assessment fee of $71 million was recognized in 2024, as the FDIC notified banks subject to the special assessment fee of the updated estimated cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund resulting from the closures in 2023 of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.

Excluding the FDIC special assessment ($203 million in 2024 versus approximately $1.7 billion in the prior year), expenses of $53.8 billion decreased 2%, driven by savings related to Citi's organizational simplification and stranded cost reduction, as well as the lower restructuring charges ($259 million in 2024 versus $781 million in the prior year) and repositioning costs.

comparisons.peer_topic: Wealth Management Non-Interest Expense Trend and Drivers
comparisons.peer_summary: Wealth Management non-interest expenses increased 5% to $20,618 million in 2024 compared to the prior year. This increase was driven by higher compensation and benefits expenses, primarily due to increased formulaic payouts to representatives on higher compensable revenues, partially offset by decreases in non-compensation expenses such as professional services, legal expenses, and FDIC special assessment costs.
comparisons.comparison: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both identify lower FDIC special assessment costs in 2024 compared to 2023 as a contributing factor to their non-compensation or non-interest expense trends. For Morgan Stanley, lower FDIC special assessment costs reduced non-compensation expenses in its Wealth Management segment. For Goldman Sachs, the reduction in FDIC fees (from $529 million in 2023 to an incremental $71 million in 2024) was a major driver of the decrease in total operating expenses. Both firms also reported higher compensation-related expenses, but the regulatory fee environment improved for both, reducing a significant prior-year burden.
